title: Block Scope
summary: Names declared with `local` live only until the end of the block they were declared in — function bodies, if/for/while bodies, do-end blocks. Outside the block they're gone; re-declaring creates a new variable.

details.heading: What is a block
details.body: Every function body, every loop body, every if/elseif/else branch, every do… end, and the chunk itself.

details.heading: Visibility rule
details.body: A local is visible from its declaration to the end of the innermost enclosing block. Inner blocks see outer locals; outer blocks can't see inner ones.

explanation.whatItIs: The fence around each local: declare inside, usable until the fence ends — no further.
explanation.whyItExists: Blocks isolate temporary names so big programs don't drown in accidental collisions.
whenToUse: Declaring loop temporaries inside the loop
do … end blocks to force early cleanup of big temporaries
Shadowing intentionally in small scopes (know you're doing it)
whenNotToUse: Expecting block locals to persist — hoist them instead
tips: Closures capture block locals — the classic counter pattern
--!strict surfaces scope mistakes as you type
commonMistakes: Declaring inside a branch, reading after it

examples.title: Fences in action
examples.code:
do
    local temp = 42
    print(temp)      --> 42
end
-- print(temp)        ← error: temp ended with the block

local total = 0
for i = 1, 3 do      -- i lives only inside the loop
    total += i
end
-- print(i)           ← error

-- Closures keep their block's locals alive:
local function counter()
    local n = 0
    return function()
        n += 1
        return n
    end
end
local c = counter()
print(c(), c())      --> 1  2
